description: See which glacial lakes become dangerous as the world warms, and who needs to act first.
summary: GlacierWatch is a web app that rates glacial lakes in Nepal by outburst-flood susceptibility and shows how warming changes the selected lake’s rating. It uses NASA POWER temperature and precipitation for 1985-2026, evaluated with the Mann-Kendall (Hamed-Rao) test and the Theil-Sen slope, and Landsat and Sentinel-2 imagery (via Microsoft Planetary Computer) to estimate lake area from selected epochs beginning in 1990. A temperature slider (+0.5 to +4 °C) drives a degree-day melt model that updates the selected lake’s volume and rating. Hazard, exposure and vulnerability are combined into a Low to Very High rating with a plain-language action for officials. A guided “Data Detective” flow walks users from the data to a verdict, and a 3D map shows a flood scenario band that scales with the warming scenario, with downstream villages and estimated arrival times. This is a susceptibility rating, not a prediction of when a lake will burst. Some model inputs, such as glacier area and melt rates, are placeholders awaiting calibration, and the flood band is a scenario band, not a hydraulic simulation.
details:
1. What does it do ?

GlacierWatch is an end-to-end climate intelligence and early warning platform designed to detect long-term climate change signals and assess the risk of catastrophic Glacial Lake Outburst Floods (GLOFs) in the high-altitude Nepal Himalaya (focusing on critically dangerous lakes such as Tsho Rolpa, Imja Tsho, and Thulagi).

The platform operates through a multi-stage scientific pipeline:

  • Climate Trend Detection: It ingests 40 years of continuous daily surface temperature (T2M) and precipitation (PRECTOTCORR) records (1985–2025) directly from the NASA POWER API. Using non-parametric Mann-Kendall trend tests, Hamed-Rao serial correlation adjustments, and Theil-Sen slope estimators, it separates statistically significant long-term climate warming and monsoon intensification from seasonal weather noise. A Positive Degree-Day (PDD) melt model then projects future meltwater volumes under different warming scenarios.
  • Multi-Decadal Lake Perimeter Delineation: Using the Microsoft Planetary Computer STAC API, the system automatically pulls multi-spectral imagery across two satellite eras: USGS/NASA Landsat (1990–2018) and ESA Sentinel-2 (2018–2026). It computes the Modified Normalized Difference Water Index (MNDWI) to delineate surface water boundaries and quantify multi-decadal expansion.
  • Hydrodynamic Dam-Breach & Downstream Routing: If an unstable moraine collapses, the system runs Froehlich’s empirical dam-breach equations to calculate peak breach discharge (QpQ_pQp​) based on water volume and moraine geometry. It then routes flood hydrographs along Copernicus 30m Digital Elevation Models (COP-DEM-GLO-30) to calculate water velocities, downstream arrival times, and flood heights.
  • Exposure Mapping & Interactive Visuals: Outburst corridors are matched with OpenStreetMap civil data to map exact distances to downstream villages, bridges, schools, and hydropower plants, displayed through an interactive 3D Mapbox GL digital twin and narrative scrollytelling experience.

2. What benefits does it have?

  • From Post-Disaster Reaction to Proactive Preparedness: Traditional monitoring often detects GLOFs only after a breach or relies on static, outdated surveys. GlacierWatch connects 40-year climate trends to immediate breach simulations, offering advance foresight.
  • Downstream Life & Asset Protection: It quantifies critical lead times (e.g., “Flood arrival at Village A in 42 minutes; peak water depth 6.8m”), giving civil defense and local authorities actionable evacuation windows.
  • Hydropower & Infrastructure Safeguarding: The Himalayan river corridors house massive clean energy and hydropower investments. GlacierWatch identifies critical infrastructure in direct flood paths for engineering retrofits and operational shutdowns.
  • Democratized Climate Science: Instead of keeping satellite data trapped in academic research papers or complex GIS software, it packages complex hydrodynamics and remote sensing into an intuitive, interactive 3D interface for community planners and decision-makers.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

The intended impact is to eliminate surprise catastrophic casualties and minimize infrastructure collapse from high-altitude glacial lake hazards across the Hindu Kush Himalaya. By providing localized, data-backed evidence of climate velocity and flood impact:

  • Local Governments & Municipalities can enact risk-informed zoning laws and set up downstream early-warning sirens.
  • Disaster Risk Reduction (DRR) Agencies can conduct targeted evacuation drills and prioritize structural lake-lowering interventions (e.g., siphoning or spillway excavation).
  • Clean Energy Operators can de-risk multi-million-dollar hydropower projects along glacial river systems.

4. What tools did we use?

  • Backend & Data Science: Python 3.11, FastAPI, NumPy, SciPy (Mann-Kendall & Theil-Sen statistical implementations), Rasterio, GeoPandas, Shapely, Pydantic, Uvicorn Assisted by Claude, Gemini, Chatgpt.
  • Space Data & Cloud APIs: NASA POWER Project REST API (NASA Langley), Microsoft Planetary Computer STAC API, USGS/NASA Landsat (Collection 2 Level-2), ESA Copernicus Sentinel-2 (L2A), Copernicus Global DEM (COP-DEM-GLO-30), OpenStreetMap Overpass API.
  • Frontend & 3D Visualization: React 18, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Mapbox GL JS (3D terrain mesh, hillshading, dynamic camera pitching), Chart.js / Recharts for statistical time-series, Lucide Icons, Assisted by Claude, Gemini, Chatgpt.
  • Development & Version Control: Git, GitHub, VS Code, POSIX/macOS development environments.

5. How is our project creative?

  • Bridge Between Climate Reanalysis and Hydrodynamic Physics: Most tools either focus purely on climate statistics or isolated flood simulations. GlacierWatch creates a seamless causal pipeline: NASA Climate Reanalysis → Glacial Lake Volume Expansion → Dam Breach Mechanics → 3D Downstream Flood Routing → Human Exposure.
  • Scientific Rigor Over Heuristics: Rather than simple linear regressions, we implemented Hamed-Rao modified Mann-Kendall tests to eliminate false trends caused by climate autocorrelation, paired with established civil engineering dam-breach physics (Froehlich).
  • Scrollytelling & 3D Immersion: Complex geospatial datasets (water indexes, contour DEMs, hydrographs) are transformed into a narrative-driven 3D digital twin, making high-altitude hazards immediately tangible to non-technical users and policymakers.

6. What factors did our team consider?

  • Extreme High-Altitude Geography & Cloud Cover: Himalayan terrain suffers from severe cloud obscuration and snow shadows. We integrated both Landsat and Sentinel-2 multi-sensor coverage paired with MNDWI thresholding to overcome cloud noise.
  • Autocorrelation in Climate Time-Series: Climate data often displays cyclical autocorrelation (e.g., El Niño / Monsoon cycles) that skews trend detection. We applied Hamed-Rao variance correction to guarantee that reported warming rates are statistically genuine.
  • Bandwidth Constraints in Vulnerable Regions: Himalayan disaster management stations often operate on low-bandwidth networks. We engineered the platform with aggressive server-side caching of NASA POWER data and lightweight GeoJSON vector delivery so it runs smoothly even on standard field laptops.
  • Socio-Economic Downstream Vulnerability: Physical flood heights mean nothing without context; we factored in critical human assets, bridges connecting isolated valleys, local schools, and hydropower dams, using an Analytical Hierarchy Process (AHP) risk matrix to prioritize areas in highest danger.
